opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because in robotics you really need both, and the tension between them is actually productive if you manage it well.

On the top-down side, I think leadership's job is to set a small number of very ambitious, clearly articulated goals. For us, that's been things like: can a robot learn general-purpose manipulation skills, can it understand natural-language instructions, can we make the same model work across different robot bodies. These are north stars. They're big enough that nobody can solve them alone, and they force different teams to share infrastructure, data, and evaluation. Without that kind of direction, a robotics lab can easily fragment into fifty small projects, each producing a nice paper, but nothing that compounds. And robotics is expensive. Hardware, data collection, operators, safety reviews. You can't afford to spread those resources too thin.

But at the same time, some of the most important breakthroughs we've had came from the bottom up. Someone notices that a vision-language model can be repurposed to output robot actions, or someone tries a weird sim-to-real trick on a weekend and it just works. Researchers who are close to the robots and the data often see the opportunity before management does. If you over-plan, you kill exactly that kind of serendipity.

So the way I try to balance it is roughly this. First, the big bets are top-down, but how to get there is mostly bottom-up. We say what we want the robot to be able to do, and we give people a lot of freedom in the technical approach. Second, I try to protect a portion of everyone's time, and some dedicated people, for exploratory work that isn't tied to the main roadmap. Third, and this is important, we have a mechanism to promote bottom-up ideas. When a small exploration shows a strong signal, we're willing to pour resources into it quickly, sometimes even reorganize around it. The transformer-based robot policy work is a good example of something that started small and then became central.

And finally, shared infrastructure is what makes both possible. If everyone uses the same data pipeline, the same robots, the same evaluation, then a bottom-up idea can be tested at scale very cheaply, and a top-down goal can actually absorb those contributions. In a way, good infrastructure is the bridge between the two.

I'd also say the balance shifts over time. When the field is in a very exploratory phase, you lean more bottom-up. When a paradigm emerges, like now with large foundation models for robotics, you lean more top-down to scale it. The art is recognizing which phase you're in.

r002.rationale: It explains that promising bottom-up explorations can quickly receive more resources or become central, citing robot policy work that started small and became central.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. This is honestly one of the questions I think about the most, because in robotics the tension is especially sharp. The field moves so fast that if you plan everything top-down, by the time the plan is executed, the world has already shifted. But if everything is bottom-up, you end up with twenty beautiful demos that don't add up to anything.

The way I think about it is that top-down sets the direction, and bottom-up decides the path. From the top, my job is to be very clear about the north star: what problem are we trying to solve, and why does it matter? For us, that's about making robots that can learn general skills and operate in the real world, not just in a lab. That direction has to be stable. It shouldn't change every quarter just because a new paper came out.

But within that direction, I try to leave a lot of room. The researchers are the ones closest to the problem. They see what's actually breaking, what data is actually missing, which idea is actually promising. If I over-specify, I lose all of that signal. So many of our best projects started as something a researcher just believed in and wanted to try, and I gave them space and some compute, and it turned into something central.

There are a few practical things that help. One is to make the direction concrete enough to be useful but not so concrete that it dictates the method. "We want a policy that can do these tasks in a new home it has never seen" is a direction. "Use this architecture with this amount of data" is not a direction, that's a solution, and I shouldn't be the one prescribing it.

Second, I try to spend a lot of time just listening. Reading people's experiments, sitting in the lab, asking what surprised them this week. Bottom-up only works if the information actually flows up. If I'm only hearing polished updates in meetings, I'm making top-down decisions based on stale information.

And third, there's a point where you have to converge. Exploration is great, but at some stage someone has to say, this is the bet, let's put most of our effort behind it. That's a top-down call, and I think leaders sometimes avoid making it because they want to be nice to everyone's project. But not deciding is also a decision, and usually a worse one.

So I don't think of it as a fixed ratio. Early in a project, it's mostly bottom-up. As things crystallize, it becomes more top-down. And then once that's done, you open it up again. It breathes. The mistake is trying to freeze it in one mode.

astra-6.text:
I think you need both. Top-down direction gives the team a shared sense of what we’re trying to achieve and which problems matter most. But research has a lot of uncertainty, so you don’t want to prescribe every technical step. The people working directly on a problem often have the best ideas about how to solve it.

So I try to be clear about the goal while giving researchers room to explore different approaches. Then we use experiments and discussion to connect those two levels. If a bottom-up result challenges our assumptions, we should be willing to adjust the direction. And if an approach isn’t working, we should be honest about that and rethink it.

To me, the balance is alignment on the problem, freedom in the approach, and a willingness to update based on evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need both. Top-down direction gives the team a shared sense of what we’re trying to achieve and which problems matter most. But research has a lot of uncertainty, so you also need room for people to explore ideas from the bottom up, challenge assumptions, and discover approaches that weren’t part of the original plan.

The balance is to be clear about the goal without prescribing every step. Then you keep a feedback loop: what researchers learn should influence the direction, and the direction should help researchers decide which ideas to pursue. In robotics, getting things to work on the real robot is a useful way to bring those two perspectives together.
